## Proof

**Setup.** Let $\mathbf{P}(E)$ be a projective space of dimension $n\ge 2$, so $\dim E = n+1$. A hyperplane $H\subset\mathbf{P}(E)$ is the projectivization of a hyperplane (a codimension-$1$ linear subspace) of $E$, hence is given by a nonzero linear form
$$\ell(X_1,\dots,X_{n+1}) = a_1 X_1 + \cdots + a_{n+1} X_{n+1} = 0,$$
with $(a_1:\cdots:a_{n+1})\in\mathbf{P}(E^*)$ determined up to a nonzero scalar. Thus hyperplanes of $\mathbf{P}(E)$ are parametrized by $\mathbf{P}(E^*)\cong\mathbf{P}^n$.

**The equation.** Let $P_i=(u_1^i:\cdots:u_{n+1}^i)$, $i=1,\dots,n$. Define the $(n+1)\times(n+1)$ determinant
$$\Delta(X) \;=\; \det\begin{pmatrix} X_1 & X_2 & \cdots & X_{n+1} \\ u_1^1 & u_2^1 & \cdots & u_{n+1}^1 \\ u_1^2 & u_2^2 & \cdots & u_{n+1}^2 \\ \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\ u_1^n & u_2^n & \cdots & u_{n+1}^n \end{pmatrix}.$$

Expanding $\Delta$ along the first row gives
$$\Delta(X) = \sum_{j=1}^{n+1} (-1)^{1+j}\, M_j\, X_j,$$
where $M_j$ is the $n\times n$ minor obtained by deleting the first row and $j$-th column. Hence $\Delta$ is a linear form in $X_1,\dots,X_{n+1}$.

**$\Delta$ is not identically zero (so it defines a hyperplane).** The $n$ points $P_1,\dots,P_n$ are projectively independent in $\mathbf{P}^n$, which means their representative vectors $v_i=(u_1^i,\dots,u_{n+1}^i)\in E$ are linearly independent. Therefore the $n$ rows $v_1,\dots,v_n$ of the submatrix formed by rows $2,\dots,n+1$ are linearly independent, so this $n\times(n+1)$ matrix has rank $n$. Consequently at least one $n\times n$ minor $M_j$ is nonzero, so $\Delta$ is a nonzero linear form. Thus $H:\Delta(X)=0$ is a well-defined hyperplane.

**Each $P_i$ lies on $H$.** Substituting $X = v_i$ (the coordinates of $P_i$) into the first row makes row $1$ equal to row $i+1$ of the determinant. A determinant with two equal rows vanishes, so $\Delta(v_i)=0$, i.e. $P_i\in H$. This holds for every $i=1,\dots,n$.

**Uniqueness.** A hyperplane of $\mathbf{P}^n$ is a projective subspace of dimension $n-1$. The $n$ projectively independent points $P_1,\dots,P_n$ span a projective subspace of dimension $n-1$ (their representative vectors span an $n$-dimensional linear subspace of $E$, whose projectivization has dimension $n-1$). Hence the projective span $\langle P_1,\dots,P_n\rangle$ is itself a hyperplane, and any hyperplane containing all $n$ points must contain this span. Since both are $(n-1)$-dimensional projective subspaces, they coincide:
$$H = \langle P_1,\dots,P_n\rangle.$$

Equivalently, the condition $P_i\in H$ translates, for each $i$, into the linear equation $\sum_{j=1}^{n+1} a_j u_j^i = 0$ on the coefficient vector $(a_1,\dots,a_{n+1})\in E^*$. These are $n$ homogeneous linear equations in $n+1$ unknowns. Projective independence of the $P_i$ means the $n$ vectors $v_i$ are linearly independent, so the $n\times(n+1)$ coefficient matrix $(u_j^i)$ has rank $n$, and the solution space in $E^*$ is $1$-dimensional. Projectivizing, there is exactly one hyperplane. The determinant $\Delta$ above is a generator of this $1$-dimensional solution space (its coefficients $(-1)^{1+j}M_j$ solve the system since each $M_j$-expansion corresponds to the cofactor structure), so $H:\Delta=0$ is the unique hyperplane.

**Conclusion.** The unique hyperplane containing the $n$ projectively independent points $P_1,\dots,P_n$ is
$$\boxed{\;\det\begin{pmatrix} X_1 & X_2 & \cdots & X_{n+1} \\ u_1^1 & u_2^1 & \cdots & u_{n+1}^1 \\ \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\ u_1^n & u_2^n & \cdots & u_{n+1}^n \end{pmatrix} = 0\;}$$
i.e. the determinant of the $(n+1)\times(n+1)$ matrix whose first row is the indeterminate $(X_1,\dots,X_{n+1})$ and whose remaining $n$ rows are the homogeneous coordinates of $P_1,\dots,P_n$.

### PROOF COMPLETE
